prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- Husbands are allowed to slap their wives if they spend lavishly, a Saudi judge said recently during a seminar on domestic violence, Saudi media reported Sunday. It is OK to slap Saudi women who spend too much, a judge has told an audience. Arab News, a Saudi English-language daily newspaper based in Riyadh, reported that Judge Hamad Al-Razine said that "if a person gives SR 1,200 [$320] to his wife and she spends 900 riyals [$240] to purchase an abaya [the black cover that women in Saudi Arabia must wear] from a brand shop and if her husband slaps her on the face as a reaction to her action, she deserves that punishment." Women in the audience immediately and loudly protested Al-Razine's statement, and were shocked to learn the remarks came from a judge, the newspaper reported. Arab News reported that Al-Razine made his remark as he was attempting to explain why incidents of domestic violence had increased in Saudi Arabia. He said that women and men shared responsibility, but added that "nobody puts even a fraction of blame" on women, the newspaper said. Al-Razine "also pointed out that women's indecent behavior and use of offensive words against their husbands were some of the reasons for domestic violence in the country," it added. Domestic violence, which used to be a taboo subject in the conservative kingdom, has become a hot topic in recent years. Groups like the National Family Safety Program have campaigned to educate the public about the problem and help prevent domestic abuse. Saudi women's rights activist Wajeha Al-Huwaider told CNN that Saudi women routinely face such attitudes. "This is how men in Saudi Arabia see women," she said in a telephone interview from the Saudi city of Dahran. "It's not something they read in a book or learned from a friend. They've been raised to see women this way, that they're less than a person." Al-Huwaider added that "I'm not surprised to see a judge or a religious man saying that - they've been raised in the same culture - a culture that tells them it's ok to raise your hand to a woman that this works." Another Saudi judge, in the city of Onaiza, was the source of a separate recent controversy: he twice denied a request from the mother of an 8-year-old girl that the girl be granted a divorce from her 47-year-old husband. Last month, after human-groups condemned the union, the girl was granted the divorce.

*A news report examining social attitudes, legal perspectives, and activist voices*

## Background

Saudi Arabia has undergone significant social and legal changes over the past decade, particularly regarding women's rights. Reforms have included granting women the right to drive (2018), easing guardianship restrictions, and expanding workforce participation. However, these changes exist alongside ongoing debates about deeply rooted social attitudes and the pace of reform.

## Historical Context on Judicial Remarks

Discussions about domestic abuse in Saudi Arabia gained international attention following incidents where public figures made controversial statements. In 2009, a family court judge, Hamad Al-Razine, drew widespread criticism when, during a seminar on domestic violence, he reportedly suggested that men had the right to discipline wives who engaged in excessive spending—remarks that critics said appeared to justify physical abuse. The comments sparked significant backlash from human rights organizations and Saudi reform advocates alike, becoming a reference point in debates about how the judicial system addresses domestic violence.

Such statements highlighted tensions between conservative interpretations of religious and social norms and growing calls for legal protections for women.

## Activist Perspectives: Wajeha Al-Huwaider

Wajeha Al-Huwaider is one of Saudi Arabia's most prominent women's rights activists, known for her advocacy dating back to the early 2000s. She gained international recognition for filming herself driving in 2008 to protest the then-existing ban on women driving—a video that circulated widely online.

Al-Huwaider has been a vocal critic of the male guardianship system, which historically required women to obtain permission from a male relative for many activities. She has framed the guardianship system as a fundamental barrier to women's autonomy, describing its effects on women's daily lives and independence.

Her activism, however, has also involved personal and legal consequences. In 2013, she and fellow activist Fawzia Al-Oyouni were convicted on charges related to their attempt to assist a woman they believed was in a dangerous domestic situation—a case that drew criticism from international human rights groups who saw it as retaliation against activism.

## Ongoing Reforms and Debates

In recent years, Saudi authorities have introduced measures aimed at addressing domestic violence, including a 2013 law criminalizing abuse and awareness campaigns such as the notable "No More Abuse" advertisement featuring an image of a veiled woman with a visible bruise. Supporters point to these steps as evidence of genuine progress.

Critics and some activists argue that enforcement remains inconsistent and that cultural attitudes evolve more slowly than laws. They note that some reforms have coincided with continued restrictions on the very activists who championed change.

## Broader Significance

The tension between reform and traditional attitudes reflects a society navigating rapid transformation. Government initiatives under Vision 2030 have emphasized expanding women's economic roles, while human rights organizations continue to monitor issues related to detained activists and the practical implementation of protections.
